chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad from Saif ibn 'Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who began with the Sa'y (walking) between As-Safa and Al-Marwah. He said, "He returns and performs Tawaf (circumambulation) of the House, then he restarts the Sa'y." I said, "That has already passed for him." He said, "He must offer a Dam (sacrifice). Do you not see that if you wash your left side before your right side, you must return and wash your left side?"

But if he began with Tawaf, performed some circuits, then forgot and stopped the Tawaf, and performed two Sa'ys between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, then remembered, he should stop the Sa'y and return to the House to complete his Tawaf, then return to the Sa'y and build upon what was cut off. The difference between this and what we mentioned earlier is that whoever began with Sa'y before Tawaf has not begun with what Allah began with, and Tawaf and restarting Sa'y became obligatory upon him. And this latter one has begun with Tawaf as Allah commanded him; it is permissible for him to build his Sa'y upon what was cut off, and this has been narrated.

key_terms.أَشْوَاط: Ashwat: Circuits (plural of shawt) of Tawaf
key_terms.الدَّم: Dam: A sacrificial animal offered as expiation for ritual errors
key_terms.السَّعْي: Sa'y: The ritual walking between the hills of Safa and Marwah
key_terms.الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَة: As-Safa and Al-Marwah: The two hills between which pilgrims walk
key_terms.الطَّوَاف: Tawaf: The ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a pilgrim performs Sa'y before completing Tawaf during Hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between starting with Sa'y versus starting with Tawaf, emphasizing that Tawaf is the foundational pillar (*rukn*) of Hajj as commanded by Allah. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) uses the analogy of washing the left hand before the right to illustrate the necessity of restoring the proper sequence, thereby ensuring the validity of the ritual order (*tartib*). The ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on strict adherence to the divine order of rituals, where deviation from the prescribed sequence requires correction and expiation.
